claims.text: A deep-learning potential trained by active learning on ab initio liquid and solid configurations near melting will improve reference–target phase-space overlap in multicomponent high-entropy alloys.
The proposed potential will reduce thermodynamic-integration path mismatch relative to EAM references.
High-entropy alloys are multicomponent systems with five or more principal elements.
The intervention should replace TOR-TILD's EAM reference with an actively trained deep neural-network potential.
The training configurations should include both near-melting liquid and solid ab initio states.
The applicable range is approximately 0.9–1.0 times the alloy melting temperature.
Liquid-phase atomic-configuration diversity is most pronounced at approximately 0.9–1.0 times the melting temperature.
Active learning can iteratively refine a deep-learning potential for high-temperature solid and liquid phases.
The deep-learning potential will capture the numerous and complex local configurations of an ab initio alloy liquid.
Capturing these local configurations will enhance overlap between the reference-potential and ab initio target phase spaces.
Machine-learned energies and forces will represent atomic dynamics more accurately than the EAM model.
The intervention may reduce TI path mismatch by approximately 30–50% relative to TOR-TILD's EAM references.
The intervention will improve the accuracy of computed free energies across the solid–liquid transition.
TOR-TILD's EAM references underestimate the diversity of atomic configurations in the ab initio liquid.
The intervention will be most effective for compositionally complex high-entropy alloys under near-melting conditions.
Deep-learning potentials have been trained using DFT calculations to describe both solid and liquid high-entropy Ti-Zr-Ta-Hf-Nb carbonitrides.
Evidence from high-entropy carbonitrides supports improved reference–target phase-space representation for multicomponent metallic high-entropy alloys.
Failure to reduce TI path mismatch by at least approximately 30% relative to the EAM reference is proposed as a falsification criterion.
Failure to improve agreement of melting free energies with independent ab initio benchmarks is proposed as an additional falsification criterion.
